title: Millionaire Mark Bouris delivers urgent wake up call to the Albanese government
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Millionaire Mark Bouris delivers urgent wake up call to the Albanese government - as he reveals why interest rates are soaring: 'Our government is spending more than it receives'

Millionaire Mark Bouris has warned the Albanese government.

Actual Article Body:
By SARAH BROOKES - SENIOR REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  11:56 AEST, 1 October 2026   |  Updated:  12:36 AEST, 1 October 2026

Millionaire Mark Bouris has warned the Albanese government’s borrowing will leave Australians’ children and grandchildren with the debt, arguing a recession may be the only way to bring inflation under control.

Australian Bureau of Statistics figures released on Wednesday showed inflation had climbed to 4 per cent, just a day after the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates for the fourth time this year.

In response, Bouris said the Labor government was living beyond its means by spending more than it collects in tax and borrowing billions to cover the gap, as Australia’s gross debt exceeded $1 trillion in August for the first time.

'The government is spending 26.9 per cent of GDP, that's the highest share of the economy any Australian government has ever spent,' he told Nine's Today show on Wednesday.

'Yet it only raises 24.1 per cent of GDP through tax. So there's a gap every year and, you know how we fill that gap...We borrow it.'

The entrepreneur argued government deficits were adding demand to the economy at the same time the Reserve Bank was trying to cool inflation through higher interest rates.

'What if I said to you, "Why are you out there spending all your family's money, all the money you earn, buying televisions, going on trips to Bali, having barbecues in the backyard, and there's a gap between what you earn and what you spend, so you borrow the money?"' Bouris said.

'And when you pass away, your kids are going to inherit that debt. What do you think that means for your kids? That means your kids are going to have to pay off your debt for the rest of their life.

Mark Bouris (pictured) has warned the Albanese government's borrowing will leave Australians' children and grandchildren saddled with the bill

The Albanese government argues spending measures are helping households manage cost-of-living pressures, while funding commitments in health, aged care, defence and the NDIS have pushed expenditure higher

'That's what's happening in our country right now. Our government is spending more than it receives, so it has to borrow.

'And my kids, my grandchildren, your kids, your grandchildren, they're going to be paying off this debt for the rest of their lives.

'That is not intergenerational equity. That's inequity.'

The Albanese government argues spending measures are helping households manage cost-of-living pressures, while funding commitments in health, aged care, defence and the NDIS have pushed expenditure higher.

The latest inflation rate remains well above the Reserve Bank's 2 to 3 per cent target band and has strengthened expectations of another rate rise in November.

Australia now has the second-highest cash rate among comparable advanced economies, behind only Iceland at 8 per cent.

Bouris said he was concerned Australia's inflation problem could ultimately require a recession to solve, as happened during the early 1990s downturn, which was famously described by then-treasurer Paul Keating as 'the recession we had to have'.

'In other words, the only way to cure this galloping inflation, which has come about as a result of too much spending, which is exactly what happened after the Hawke-Keating government, too much spending, was to have a recession to fix the inflation problem.

RBA governor Michele Bullock (pictured) on Tuesday stopped short of ruling out another rate hike before Christmas if fresh shocks hit the economy

How should we balance support for families today with the debt left to future generations?

'And the recession came about as a result of the Reserve Bank hiking interest rates to the highest interest rates we've ever had.

Bouris argued 'galloping inflation', driven by excessive spending, could only be brought under control through a significant economic slowdown.
